label: US farm-animal sales laws and the fight against a federal override (ours)

rows.label: Share of Americans living in states that ban sales of eggs from caged hens

source.title: USDA Economic Research Service, Amber Waves (April 2023)
source.quote: by 2026 more than 23 percent of the U.S. population would reside in States with retail sales restrictions

rows.explainer: California, Colorado, Massachusetts, Michigan, Nevada, Oregon and Washington, the seven states ERS counts; an override of state sales laws, as in the EATS and 'Save Our Bacon' Acts, would undo them. Eggs are eaten roughly in proportion to population, so about this share of US hens supply those states. ERS says 'more than' 23%; Arizona, Utah and Rhode Island have laws too (about 3.5 points more), the high end.

rows.label: California's share of the US population, 2024

source.title: US Census Bureau, QuickFacts: California; United States (Vintage 2024 estimates)

rows.explainer: 39,431,263 of 340,110,988 people: scales the egg part of Proposition 12's cost from California to every state with an egg sales law.

rows.label: Breeding sows supplying California under Proposition 12

source.title: Holly Cook (National Pork Producers Council), testimony to the House Agriculture Committee, July 2025
source.quote: approximately 700,000 sows would be needed to meet historical demand levels in California
source.note: Low end: National Hog Farmer, 'What's Prop 12 really costing producers, consumers?' (2024, nationalhogfarmer.com/market-news/what-s-prop-12-really-costing-producers-consumers-), says anecdotal evidence points to about 400,000 compliant sows at 1 January 2024, enough for about 60% of California's historical pork consumption; the site refuses automated fetches, so read from search summaries (retrieved 2026-11-15).

rows.explainer: Sows housed to Proposition 12's standard to supply California, which the 'Save Our Bacon' Act would undo (Massachusetts's Question 3 adds a little, inside the range). Best guess the 700,000 the pork producers say California's demand needs; low end the about 400,000 reported compliant when enforcement began (2024); high end allows for Massachusetts and for supply growing to meet demand. Veal calves, also covered (and in the cost), are left out: the veal market supplying California is small (our judgment, a few tens of thousands of calves a year).

rows.label: Share of Proposition 12's net compliance cost that falls on eggs

source.title: California Department of Food and Agriculture (2021), Animal Confinement: Notice of Proposed Action
source.quote: Egg producers in California face higher costs by $72 million

rows.explainer: Our judgment, splitting @compliance_costs.ca_prop12_net_cost_per_year: the notice puts most of the gross on eggs ($40 of $50 a person), but retailers' extra egg margin (about $970 million, a transfer) is nearly all of that egg spending, so we take the net egg part to be about the size of California's egg producers' $72 million (less the $7 million more farm revenue the notice also gives) against the roughly $300 million net: 0.25. The net is built from spending and the Department of Finance notes producers' costs are not quantified, so this is a judgment, not an identity. Range 0.05 to 0.5.

rows.label: Share of the animals under the state sales laws that would go back into cages or crates within the years counted if the laws fell
rows.explainer: Our judgment: the federal bills (EATS, 'Save Our Bacon') would void the states' rules for eggs and pork produced elsewhere; in-state housing laws and company pledges would keep most cage-free and crate-free supply, and barns already built rarely go back to cages; replacement barns, buyers without pledges and price pressure after bird flu would bring some back.

rows.label: Share of the risk of a federal override of the state sales laws that the coalition's 2025 opposition removed
rows.explainer: Our judgment: the year's opposition (letters from more than 200 members of Congress against the EATS language, testimony and farmer outreach before the July 2025 House hearing) takes about 5 points off a 30% risk, a sixth of it. Research on lobbying finds most campaigns change nothing (Baumgartner and colleagues, 2009); organised constituent contact moved legislators' support by about 12 points in a field experiment (Bergan and Cole, 2015). A share of the risk, so the opposition never raises it; the override itself is one event, drawn in each model's chance without the opposition.

rows.label: Chance a federal override of the state farm-animal sales laws passes in the next Farm Bill without the coalition's 2025 opposition

source.title: The Humane League, Animal Policy Alliance year in review (February 2026)
source.quote: By the end of the year, more than 200 members of Congress had signed letters opposing the EATS language
source.note: ASPCA press release on the July 2025 House Agriculture Committee hearing on Proposition 12: https://www.aspca.org/about-us/press-releases/us-house-agriculture-committee-holds-hearing-proposition-12

rows.explainer: Our judgment. EATS-style language and the 'Save Our Bacon' Act were in the House Farm Bill drafts of 2024-25, and the Department of Justice sued California over Proposition 12 in 2025; the coalition (Humane World for Animals, the ASPCA, The Humane League and others) gathered letters from more than 200 members of Congress against them. Without that opposition we put an override in the next Farm Bill at 30%, from 10% to 50%. One event, drawn in each model as happens or doesn't; the opposition removes a share of it (us_preemption_opposition_risk_cut).

rows.label: The whole coalition's spending on defending the state sales laws against a federal override, 2025 (programme spending, before overhead)
rows.explainer: Our judgment: Humane World for Animals leads, with the ASPCA, The Humane League and its Animal Policy Alliance grantees, Animal Wellness Action, Mercy For Animals and others, plus farm and state allies; federal lobbying, litigation and campaigns, several times The Humane League's own ($406,653 of lobbying on every issue, Form 990 Schedule C). One pool, so each charity's credit is its own spending over the same total. $8.5 million, $3.5 million to $20.5 million.
